blocks.body:
Suppose someone hands you an infinite list of polynomial equations in three unknowns, say $f_1 = 0, f_2 = 0, f_3 = 0, \dots$, and asks for the common solutions. Is the infinite list really needed, or could you always throw away all but finitely many equations without changing the answer? In 1890 Hilbert proved that a finite sub-list always suffices. The algebraic property behind this is called being Noetherian, after Emmy Noether, who saw that one simple finiteness condition on ideals drives a large part of commutative algebra.

This page gives three equivalent definitions, proves Hilbert's basis theorem, and shows what the condition buys. Throughout, ring means commutative ring with $1$, as on the page on [[rings]].

In the integers every ideal has the form $(n) = n\mathbb{Z}$, so one generator is enough. The same is true in $k[x]$ for a field $k$, because both rings are principal ideal domains: an ideal is generated by any of its nonzero elements of smallest size (absolute value, or degree).

For two variables this fails: the ideal $(x, y) \subseteq k[x,y]$ of polynomials with zero constant term is not principal. A single generator $g$ would have to divide both $x$ and $y$, forcing $g$ to be a nonzero constant, but then $(g)$ would be the whole ring, which contains $1 \notin (x,y)$. Still, two generators suffice. The question is whether some finite number of generators always suffices.

It does not in every ring. Let $R = k[x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots]$ be the polynomial ring in infinitely many variables (each polynomial uses only finitely many of them). The ideal $I = (x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots)$ is not finitely generated: finitely many elements of $I$ involve only $x_1, \dots, x_n$ for some $n$, and we will see in Example 1 that $x_{n+1}$ is then not in the ideal they generate. Equivalently, the chain
$$(x_1) \subsetneq (x_1, x_2) \subsetneq (x_1, x_2, x_3) \subsetneq \cdots$$
climbs forever. These two symptoms, an ideal needing infinitely many generators and an ascending chain of ideals that never stops, turn out to be the same disease.

blocks.title: Noetherian ring
Equivalence of the three conditions
blocks.body: For a ring $R$, the three conditions in the definition are equivalent.

(1) implies (2). Let $I_1 \subseteq I_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be a chain and let $I = \bigcup_n I_n$. This union is an ideal: if $a, b \in I$ then $a \in I_m$ and $b \in I_n$, and both lie in $I_{\max(m,n)}$, so $a - b$ and $ra$ lie in $I$. By (1), $I = (a_1, \dots, a_r)$. Each $a_j$ lies in some $I_{n_j}$; put $N = \max_j n_j$. Then all $a_j \in I_N$, so $I \subseteq I_N \subseteq I_n \subseteq I$ for every $n \ge N$, and the chain is constant from $N$ on.

(2) implies (3). Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a nonempty collection of ideals with no maximal element. Pick $I_1 \in \mathcal{S}$. Since $I_1$ is not maximal in $\mathcal{S}$ there is $I_2 \in \mathcal{S}$ with $I_1 \subsetneq I_2$, then $I_3 \in \mathcal{S}$ with $I_2 \subsetneq I_3$, and so on. This chain never stabilises, contradicting (2).

(3) implies (1). Let $I$ be an ideal and let $\mathcal{S}$ be the collection of finitely generated ideals contained in $I$. It is nonempty, since $(0) \in \mathcal{S}$, so it has a maximal element $J = (a_1, \dots, a_r)$. If some $a \in I$ were not in $J$, then $(a_1, \dots, a_r, a)$ would be a finitely generated ideal inside $I$ strictly larger than $J$, contradicting maximality. Hence $I = J$ is finitely generated.

Fields and principal ideal domains such as $\mathbb{Z}$, $k[x]$ and the Gaussian integers are Noetherian, since every ideal has one generator. Two closure properties make it easy to produce many more examples.

Quotients. If $R$ is Noetherian and $I$ is an ideal, then $R/I$ is Noetherian. The ideals of $R/I$ correspond, preserving inclusion, to the ideals of $R$ that contain $I$ (the correspondence theorem from [[rings]]), so an ascending chain in $R/I$ lifts to an ascending chain in $R$, which stops.

Polynomial rings. This is Hilbert's theorem, proved below: if $R$ is Noetherian, so is $R[x]$. By induction, $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is Noetherian. Combining the two properties, every ring of the form $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]/I$ is Noetherian; these are exactly the rings generated over $R$ by finitely many elements. So $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] \cong \mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^2+5)$, $\mathbb{C}[x,y]/(y^2 - x^3)$ and every ring of integers of a number field are Noetherian.

blocks.title: Hilbert's basis theorem
blocks.body: If $R$ is a Noetherian ring, then the polynomial ring $R[x]$ is Noetherian. Consequently $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is Noetherian, and in particular every ideal of $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ ($k$ a field) and of $\mathbb{Z}[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is finitely generated.

blocks.title: Proof of Hilbert's basis theorem
blocks.body:
The idea is to control an ideal of $R[x]$ through the leading coefficients of its elements, which live in the Noetherian ring $R$.

Suppose some ideal $I \subseteq R[x]$ is not finitely generated. Choose $f_1 \in I$ of smallest possible degree among nonzero elements of $I$. Having chosen $f_1, \dots, f_k$, the ideal $(f_1, \dots, f_k)$ is not all of $I$, so choose $f_{k+1} \in I \setminus (f_1, \dots, f_k)$ of smallest possible degree. Let $d_k = \deg f_k$ and let $a_k \in R$ be the leading coefficient of $f_k$.

The degrees never decrease: $f_{k+1}$ was available at the previous step as well (it lies in $I \setminus (f_1, \dots, f_{k-1})$), so $d_k \le d_{k+1}$ by the minimal choice of $f_k$.

Now look at the chain of ideals of $R$
$$(a_1) \subseteq (a_1, a_2) \subseteq (a_1, a_2, a_3) \subseteq \cdots .$$
Since $R$ is Noetherian it stabilises, so for some $N$ we have $a_{N+1} \in (a_1, \dots, a_N)$, say $a_{N+1} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} r_i a_i$ with $r_i \in R$. Consider
$$g = f_{N+1} - \sum_{i=1}^{N} r_i\, x^{d_{N+1} - d_i} f_i .$$
The exponents $d_{N+1} - d_i$ are nonnegative because the degrees are nondecreasing. Each term $r_i x^{d_{N+1}-d_i} f_i$ has degree at most $d_{N+1}$ with coefficient $r_i a_i$ in degree $d_{N+1}$, so the coefficient of $x^{d_{N+1}}$ in $g$ is $a_{N+1} - \sum r_i a_i = 0$, and $\deg g < d_{N+1}$ (or $g = 0$).

But $g \in I$, and $g \notin (f_1, \dots, f_N)$: otherwise $f_{N+1} = g + \sum r_i x^{d_{N+1}-d_i} f_i$ would lie in $(f_1, \dots, f_N)$. In particular $g \neq 0$. So $g$ is an element of $I \setminus (f_1, \dots, f_N)$ of degree smaller than $d_{N+1}$, contradicting the choice of $f_{N+1}$. Hence every ideal of $R[x]$ is finitely generated.

The consequences follow by induction, since $R[x_1, \dots, x_n] = (R[x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}])[x_n]$, starting from the Noetherian rings $k$ and $\mathbb{Z}$.

blocks.title: What the theorem says about equations
blocks.body:
Back to the opening question. For a set $S$ of polynomials in $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$, write $V(S)$ for the set of common zeros in $k^n$. If $I$ is the ideal generated by $S$, then $V(S) = V(I)$, because any combination $\sum h_i s_i$ vanishes wherever all the $s_i$ do. By Hilbert's theorem $I = (g_1, \dots, g_r)$, and each $g_j$ is itself a combination of finitely many elements of $S$. Collecting those finitely many elements $s_1, \dots, s_m$ we get $I = (s_1, \dots, s_m)$ and therefore
$$V(S) = V(s_1, \dots, s_m).$$
Every system of polynomial equations, however large, is equivalent to a finite subsystem.

The ascending chain condition on ideals turns into a descending chain condition on solution sets: if $V_1 \supseteq V_2 \supseteq \cdots$ are zero sets of polynomials, the corresponding ideals of vanishing polynomials increase, hence stop, and so the $V_i$ stop shrinking. From this one proves that every algebraic set is a finite union of irreducible pieces, the first structural fact of algebraic geometry.

There is also an algorithmic side. Buchberger's algorithm for Gröbner bases repeatedly adds new polynomials to a list; it terminates because the ideals generated by the leading terms form an ascending chain, which must stop. Dickson's lemma (Example 3) is the monomial version of the same phenomenon.

blocks.title: Noetherian modules and further results
blocks.body:
The same finiteness makes sense for modules, the setting of [[modules]]. An $R$-module $M$ is Noetherian if every submodule is finitely generated, equivalently if ascending chains of submodules stop; a ring is Noetherian exactly when it is Noetherian as a module over itself, since its submodules are its ideals.

A standard lemma, stated here without proof: if $N \subseteq M$ is a submodule, then $M$ is Noetherian if and only if both $N$ and $M/N$ are. From this, by induction, $R^n$ is Noetherian when $R$ is, and so is every quotient of $R^n$, that is, every finitely generated $R$-module. So over a Noetherian ring, submodules of finitely generated modules are again finitely generated. For $R = \mathbb{Z}$ this says that subgroups of finitely generated abelian groups are finitely generated, a fact used silently in the structure theorem.

Primary decomposition of ideals (the Lasker–Noether theorem), Krull's intersection theorem and dimension theory all assume the Noetherian condition. Hilbert's theorem also has a power series version (again stated without proof): if $R$ is Noetherian, so is the power series ring $R[\![x]\!]$.

blocks.title: Example 1: infinitely many variables
blocks.body: Show that in $R = k[x_1, x_2, \dots]$ the chain $(x_1) \subseteq (x_1, x_2) \subseteq \cdots$ is strictly increasing, so $R$ is not Noetherian.
blocks.solution:
Fix $n$ and suppose $x_{n+1} \in (x_1, \dots, x_n)$, say $x_{n+1} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} h_i x_i$ with $h_i \in R$. Apply the ring homomorphism $\varphi\colon R \to R$ that sends $x_1, \dots, x_n$ to $0$ and fixes every other variable (substitution is a ring homomorphism). The right-hand side maps to $\sum \varphi(h_i)\cdot 0 = 0$, while the left-hand side maps to $x_{n+1} \ne 0$. Contradiction.

So $x_{n+1} \notin (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ and each inclusion is strict. The chain never stabilises, condition (2) fails, and $R$ is not Noetherian. (The same substitution shows that the ideal $(x_1, x_2, \dots)$ is not finitely generated.)

blocks.title: Example 2: a monomial ideal
blocks.body: In $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]$ let $I$ be the ideal generated by all monomials $x^i y^j$ with $i + 2j \ge 4$. Hilbert's theorem promises finitely many generators. Find them.
blocks.solution:
First a general fact. If $I$ is generated by a set of monomials, then a monomial $m$ lies in $I$ exactly when some generating monomial divides it. Indeed if $m = \sum h_k m_k$, expand every $h_k$ into monomials: each monomial appearing on the right is a multiple of some $m_k$, and $m$ itself must appear on the right after cancellation, so $m$ is a multiple of some $m_k$.

So we only need the monomials in the set that are not divisible by another one in the set: the minimal exponent pairs $(i,j)$ with $i + 2j \ge 4$ under the componentwise order. For $j = 0$ the smallest $i$ is $4$; for $j = 1$ it is $i = 2$; for $j = 2$ it is $i = 0$. Any pair with $j \ge 2$ dominates $(0,2)$, any pair with $j=1$ dominates $(2,1)$, and any pair with $j=0$ dominates $(4,0)$. Hence
$$I = (x^4,\ x^2 y,\ y^2).$$
Three generators replace infinitely many. Notice that the minimal generating set of a monomial ideal is unique, though ideals in general have many different generating sets.

blocks.title: Example 3: Dickson's lemma from the ascending chain condition
blocks.body: (Dickson's lemma, olympiad style.) Prove that in any infinite sequence $(a_1, b_1), (a_2, b_2), \dots$ of pairs of nonnegative integers there are indices $i < j$ with $a_i \le a_j$ and $b_i \le b_j$.
blocks.solution:
Encode the pairs as monomials $m_k = x^{a_k} y^{b_k}$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]$ and consider the ideals $J_k = (m_1, \dots, m_k)$. These form an ascending chain, so by Hilbert's theorem and condition (2) there is $N$ with $J_{N+1} = J_N$. Then $m_{N+1} \in (m_1, \dots, m_N)$, and by the fact from Example 2 some $m_i$ with $i \le N$ divides $m_{N+1}$, which means exactly $a_i \le a_{N+1}$ and $b_i \le b_{N+1}$. Take $j = N+1$.

The same argument works verbatim for $n$-tuples, using $\mathbb{Q}[x_1, \dots, x_n]$. (There is also an elementary proof by extracting nondecreasing subsequences coordinate by coordinate.)

blocks.body:
- A subring of a Noetherian ring can fail to be Noetherian: $k[x_1, x_2, \dots]$ is not Noetherian, yet it lies inside its field of fractions, which has only two ideals. Another classic example is the ring of rational polynomials with integer constant term, $\mathbb{Z} + x\mathbb{Q}[x]$, inside $\mathbb{Q}[x]$: there the chain $(x) \subsetneq (x/2) \subsetneq (x/4) \subsetneq \cdots$ never stops.
- Noetherian does not mean a bounded number of generators. In $k[x,y]$ the ideal $(x,y)^n$ needs $n+1$ generators $x^n, x^{n-1}y, \dots, y^n$, so no single bound works for all ideals.
- The ascending chain condition does not imply the descending one: in $\mathbb{Z}$ the chain $(2) \supsetneq (4) \supsetneq (8) \supsetneq \cdots$ never stops. Rings with the descending chain condition (Artinian rings) form a much smaller class.
- Being a UFD and being Noetherian are independent: $k[x_1, x_2, \dots]$ is a UFD but not Noetherian, and $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is Noetherian but not a UFD.

Principal ideal domains such as those on [[ufds]] and [[gaussian-integers]] are the simplest Noetherian rings. In algebraic number theory, rings of integers are Noetherian domains in which nonzero ideals factor uniquely into primes; see [[ideals]] and [[class-group]]. In algebraic geometry, Hilbert's basis theorem is what makes zero sets of polynomials manageable, and the Nullstellensatz (also due to Hilbert) then matches them with radical ideals. The modules side continues the theory on [[modules]], and the leading-coefficient idea of the proof reappears in Gröbner basis algorithms, a topic close to [[algorithms]]. The same ascending chain condition, applied to the open sets of a space, gives the notion of a Noetherian topological space, a variant of the ideas on [[topological-spaces]].

1. Show that $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ and $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]/(xy - 1)$ are Noetherian without finding any generators.
2. Find the minimal monomial generators of the ideal of $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]$ generated by all $x^i y^j$ with $ij \ge 6$.
3. Let $R$ be Noetherian and $\varphi\colon R \to R$ a surjective ring homomorphism. By looking at the chain $\ker \varphi \subseteq \ker \varphi^2 \subseteq \cdots$, prove that $\varphi$ is injective.
4. In the ring $C[0,1]$ of continuous real functions, let $I_n$ be the set of functions vanishing on $[0, 1/n]$. Show that $I_1 \subsetneq I_2 \subsetneq \cdots$, so $C[0,1]$ is not Noetherian.
